title: Creating people
author: 100% Assessment
summary: Assessment is not merely a measurement act but a construction act: every time pupils receive test results, they internalize signals about competence, comparison, and futures. Form (pass/fail, bands, percentiles) shapes self-concept; pupils describe themselves in its terms. Context makes the same score feel triumphant or shameful depending on set placement. Schools attach moral worth to success, so struggle reads as a verdict on character. Teachers are game designers: pupils who repeatedly lose internalize loser identities and behave accordingly, driven either toward instrumental optimization of the system or toward deliberate avoidance. Assessment choices have consequences for who pupils become.
points: Assessment reports do not merely measure understanding; they actively construct who pupils believe themselves to be, especially when results are tied to labels, bands, or ranks.
The form in which results are conveyed matters more than the score: being top of set 2 feels like success even at 67 percent, while bottom of set 1 feels like failure.
Schools routinely conflate academic success with moral worth and future prospects, which reads as a verdict on pupil value to those who struggle.
Achievement goal orientation shapes whether pupils play to master the domain or to perform relative to peers; repeated failure produces deliberate avoidance, not effort.
Teachers and leaders are game designers: assessment choices determine which pupils internalize winner identities and which internalize loser identities that narrow futures.
quotes: The individual in contemporary society is not so much described by tests as constructed by them (Allan Hanson, 1994)

Every time we share the results of an assessment with pupils, we add a drop in the ocean of who they believe themselves to be. We often think of testing pupils as merely a means to ascertain what they know, but we rarely stop to think how the very act also shapes their self-concept.” “These micro-exposures provide us with repeated signals about how competent we are, how we compare to others, and what we may be worthy of achieving in the future.

The form in which results are conveyed may signal to pupils what the teacher (or the school or world more widely) believes about them - that they are a ‘failure’, exceeding or falling below expectations, or high/mediocre/low performing. Pupils can internalise the form so deeply that they even begin to describe themselves in these terms: “I am a level 4” or “I’m an epic failure at maths”.

It is this effect that leads pupils to say that they would rather be at the top of set 2 in maths than at the bottom of set 1. They know that it is not so much how well they perform, but how they feel about this performance as a result of the performance of those around them.

Whether we mean to or not, educators equate success at school with moral worth. Success is attributed to hard work, those that do well in assessments receive warm words and smiles, and we reinforce at every opportunity the correlation between success at school and the chance of a fulfilling, socially valuable life.
I chose not to fight the system but to play with it. I did what I had to do to achieve my goals, I played the game, if you will. (Ruth Borland in The Irish Times, 27 September 2005)

When it comes to assessment, teachers and school leaders are the game designers. If some pupils repeatedly lose, we should not be surprised when they internalise a loser identity and behave accordingly.” Archived from 100% Assessment (Substack) on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
